triage.name: Autism Spectrum Disorder
triage.reason: Developmental presentation with impaired social communication and restricted repetitive behaviors; diagnosis by history and observation, with hearing and developmental screening in the workup.

review_issues: auto-repaired: workup: 'mri brain without contrast' was in ['supporting', 'not_indicated'], kept ['not_indicated', 'supporting']
auto-repaired: workup: 'cbc' was in initial, not_indicated; kept initial as a conditional order (only if pica, poor intake or suspected nutritional deficiency)
auto-repaired: workup: 'ferritin' was in initial, not_indicated; kept initial as a conditional order (only if pica, restricted diet or suspected iron deficiency)
auto-repaired: workup: 'tsh' was in initial, not_indicated; kept initial as a conditional order (only if growth failure, constipation, fatigue or clinical suspicion of hypothyroidism)

auto-repaired: workup: 'MRI brain without contrast' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if macrocephaly, focal neurologic findings, regression, seizures or suspected tuberous sclerosis complex)
auto-repaired: workup: 'EEG' was in supporting, not_indicated; kept supporting as a conditional order (only if clinical seizures, regression or episodic staring spells)
presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: Diagnosed about 3–4 times more often in boys than girls
Symptoms are usually recognized in the second year of life, though some children are not diagnosed until school age or adulthood
Diagnosis is made across all racial, ethnic and socioeconomic groups

risk_factors.text: Having a sibling or other first-degree relative with autism spectrum disorder
Certain genetic syndromes (for example fragile X syndrome, tuberous sclerosis complex, Rett syndrome)
Preterm birth or very low birth weight
In utero exposure to valproate or thalidomide

family_history: Autism spectrum disorder in a sibling or parent
Learning disability or language delay in a family member
Intellectual disability in a family member
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder in a family member
social_history: Often noticed first by parents or early childhood educators when milestones are not met
Difficulties may become more obvious when the child starts preschool or school and social demands increase

chief_complaints.text: He doesn't respond when I call his name
She isn't talking yet, and other kids her age are
He doesn't look at me or point at things he wants
She lines up her toys and gets very upset if I move them
He repeats the same phrases over and over
She covers her ears and screams when it gets noisy

hpi.onset: Gradual, with differences in social communication and behavior noticed in the first two years of life; parents often recall that the child was 'different' from early infancy
hpi.duration: Lifelong; concerns are typically present from early childhood and persist
hpi.progression: Social and communication difficulties become more apparent as developmental and social demands increase; restricted interests and repetitive behaviors often persist but may change in form with age
hpi.quality: A persistent pattern of difficulty with back-and-forth social interaction and communication, together with restricted, repetitive behaviors and unusually intense or narrow interests
hpi.severity: Variable, ranging from mild difficulties that are noticed mainly in social or school settings to severe impairment requiring substantial support
hpi.timing: Present across settings and most of the day, not limited to one environment
aggravating: Loud noises, bright lights or crowded settings
relieving: Time with a preferred interest or object

associated_symptoms.text: Delayed or absent speech, or loss of words previously used
Poor eye contact and not responding to name
Repetitive movements such as hand flapping, rocking or spinning
Insistence on sameness and distress with small changes
Unusual reactions to sounds, textures, lights or smells
Self-injurious behavior such as head banging or biting

pertinent_negatives: Loss of previously acquired motor or language skills after a period of normal development (regression is possible but a clear loss of skills should prompt evaluation for a neurodegenerative or metabolic cause)
Normal social smiling and joint attention by 12 months
No repetitive behaviors or restricted interests
Symptoms beginning only after a clear illness or injury
Focal neurologic deficits or loss of consciousness

positives.text: Difficulty with back-and-forth conversation and sharing interests
Repetitive behaviors or insistence on sameness

argues_against: Hearing impairment as the primary cause of language delay

atypical.how_it_differs: Young children may present only with delayed language, lack of pointing or joint attention, and repetitive play; the social difficulties may not be obvious until preschool.
missing_classic_features: Restricted interests described by the child

atypical.how_it_differs: Adults may have learned to mask social difficulties and present with anxiety, depression, or social exhaustion rather than obvious autistic behaviors; diagnosis may be made late in life.
Infants may show reduced babbling, poor eye contact, lack of social smiling, and not turning to name by 9–12 months; diagnosis is usually not made before 18–24 months.

general.mild: Well-appearing, well-nourished child; may avoid eye contact or not respond to the examiner's greeting; plays alone
general.moderate: Well-appearing but aloof; limited response to name or social overtures; repetitive movements or echoing of speech may be seen
general.severe: Markedly withdrawn, minimal or no spoken language, repetitive self-stimulatory movements, distress with changes or sensory input
general.critical: Not applicable; autism spectrum disorder is not a critical illness, though a child may present acutely with injury, seizure or severe agitation

findings.maneuver: Observe the child during the visit and attempt to engage face to face
findings.finding: Reduced or absent eye contact and limited shared attention with the examiner

findings.maneuver: Call the child's name from across the room while the child is occupied
findings.finding: Does not turn or orient to name

findings.maneuver: Point to an object across the room and watch whether the child follows the point or points back to share interest
findings.finding: Does not follow a point or use pointing to share interest (no joint attention)

findings.maneuver: Ask the caregiver about words and phrases the child uses, and attempt conversation
findings.finding: Fewer words than expected for age, absent phrase speech, or unusual speech such as echolalia

findings.maneuver: Observe the child at rest and during play
findings.finding: Repetitive movements such as hand flapping, rocking, spinning or finger flicking

findings.maneuver: Ask the caregiver what happens when routines or the arrangement of toys change
findings.finding: Marked distress or tantrum with small changes in routine or order

findings.maneuver: Ask the caregiver about the child's play and preferred topics
findings.finding: Intense, narrow interests or play limited to parts of objects

findings.maneuver: Observe the child's reaction to ordinary sounds, light or touch during the exam
findings.finding: Covers ears, startles or becomes distressed with ordinary sensory input

findings.maneuver: Perform or review a hearing screen and inspect the ears and canals
findings.finding: Normal hearing screen and normal ear exam

findings.maneuver: Assess tone, strength, deep tendon reflexes, coordination and gait
findings.finding: No focal weakness, no abnormal tone, no ataxia or focal deficit

findings.maneuver: Measure height, weight and head circumference and plot on a growth chart
findings.finding: Growth parameters tracking along expected percentiles

findings.maneuver: Inspect the face, hands and body for unusual features
findings.finding: Dysmorphic features suggesting a genetic syndrome such as fragile X or tuberous sclerosis

findings.maneuver: Examine the skin with a Wood lamp for hypopigmented macules
findings.finding: Ash-leaf spots or other lesions suggesting tuberous sclerosis complex

labs.caveat: Ordered to rule out congenital or acquired hypothyroidism as a treatable cause of developmental delay; usually normal in autism spectrum disorder.
Considered when there is regression, pica or a restricted diet; low levels are uncommon and do not explain the core social-communication deficits.
Only when there is developmental regression, lethargy, vomiting or episodic encephalopathy suggesting an inborn error of metabolism; normal in typical autism spectrum disorder.
Lumbar puncture is not part of routine autism evaluation; mildly elevated protein may be seen in some neurodegenerative or metabolic conditions that present with regression.

imaging.preferred_when: Macrocephaly, focal neurologic findings, regression, seizures or suspected tuberous sclerosis complex

findings.text: Normal brain MRI in most children with autism spectrum disorder
Tubers or subependymal nodules suggesting tuberous sclerosis complex

imaging.preferred_when: Acute head injury, new focal deficit or suspected increased intracranial pressure when MRI is unavailable

findings.text: Usually normal; may show calcified tubers in tuberous sclerosis complex

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected physical abuse or unexplained injuries

findings.text: No fractures in the absence of trauma

initial.why: Hearing loss is a common and treatable cause of language and social delay and must be excluded before attributing findings to autism spectrum disorder
Standardized screening at 18 and 24 months and whenever concerns arise identifies children who need a full evaluation
Characterizes communication strengths and deficits and guides therapy
Baseline blood count; may identify anemia or lead to further testing if pica is present
initial.only_if: pica, poor intake or suspected nutritional deficiency

initial.why: Iron deficiency is common with restricted diets and pica
initial.only_if: pica, restricted diet or suspected iron deficiency

initial.why: Hypothyroidism is a treatable cause of developmental delay
initial.only_if: growth failure, constipation, fatigue or clinical suspicion of hypothyroidism

confirmatory.why: Standardized observational assessment of social communication and repetitive behaviors used with history to confirm the diagnosis
Structured caregiver interview that documents early developmental history and current symptoms

supporting.why: Validated parent-report screening tool for toddlers; a positive screen prompts full evaluation
Measures adaptive functioning to guide support planning
First-tier test to identify copy number variants associated with autism spectrum disorder
Identifies the most common inherited cause of intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder
Evaluates structural causes when macrocephaly, focal deficits, regression or seizures are present
supporting.only_if: macrocephaly, focal neurologic findings, regression, seizures or suspected tuberous sclerosis complex

supporting.why: Evaluates for seizures or epileptiform activity
supporting.only_if: clinical seizures, regression or episodic staring spells

supporting.why: Screens for inborn errors of metabolism when there is developmental regression, lethargy or episodic symptoms
supporting.only_if: regression, lethargy, vomiting or episodic encephalopathy

not_indicated.why: No role in the routine evaluation of autism spectrum disorder
Only for suspected abuse or unexplained injury
Not routinely needed without regression, pica or a severely restricted diet
Not routinely needed without regression, lethargy or episodic encephalopathy
Lumbar puncture is not part of the routine autism evaluation

decision_points: Hearing test before attributing language delay to autism spectrum disorder
Positive developmental screen or clear caregiver concern prompts a comprehensive multidisciplinary evaluation
Regression, focal neurologic findings, macrocephaly or seizures prompt brain MRI and further etiologic testing
Genetic testing offered to all children with a confirmed diagnosis

criteria.name: Autism spectrum disorder diagnostic criteria (paraphrased)
criteria.summary: Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple settings, plus restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests or activities, present in early development and causing significant impairment. Symptoms must not be better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay.
items: Deficits in nonverbal communication used for social interaction
Deficits in developing, maintaining and understanding relationships
Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects or speech
Insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines or ritualized patterns
Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus
Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment

differential.name: Hearing loss
differential.why_considered: A child who does not respond to name, does not speak on schedule, and seems socially aloof may simply not be hearing.
differential.trigger: Any child with language delay or poor response to name

history: Responds to loud sounds or vibration but not to speech
Frequent ear infections or a family history of childhood hearing loss
Watches faces and seeks social contact, using gestures to communicate
exam: Abnormal otoscopy or tympanic membrane findings
Abnormal audiologic testing or otoacoustic emissions
Uses eye contact and joint attention normally once attention is gained
labs: Genetic testing for connexin 26 when sensorineural loss is confirmed
imaging: Temporal bone imaging when conductive or structural causes are suspected

differential.name: Intellectual disability
differential.why_considered: Delayed language and adaptive skills overlap with autism, and the two frequently co-occur.

history: Delays are global and proportional across cognitive, language and adaptive domains
Social interest and desire to interact are relatively preserved
No restricted interests or insistence on sameness
exam: Adaptive behavior scores low across all domains rather than showing a social-communication profile
May have dysmorphic features suggesting a specific syndrome
labs: Chromosomal microarray and fragile X testing to identify an underlying cause

differential.name: Social (pragmatic) communication disorder
differential.why_considered: Difficulty with the social use of language can look like the social-communication deficits of autism.

history: Difficulties limited to social use of language
No repetitive behaviors, restricted interests or insistence on sameness
No history of sensory hyper- or hyporeactivity
exam: Normal nonverbal communication and joint attention

differential.name: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
differential.why_considered: Inattention, impulsivity and difficulty with peer relationships can resemble autism, and the two commonly co-occur.

history: Symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity and impulsivity rather than social-communication deficits
Social difficulties are driven by impulsivity or inattention, not by lack of social understanding
No restricted interests or repetitive behaviors
exam: Normal eye contact and social reciprocity

differential.name: Reactive attachment disorder
differential.why_considered: Children with severe early neglect may show withdrawn, socially unresponsive behavior that resembles autism.
differential.trigger: History of severe neglect, institutional care or multiple caregiver changes

history: Clear history of severe neglect or inadequate caregiving
Social withdrawal and lack of seeking comfort from caregivers
Symptoms improve markedly when placed in a stable, responsive caregiving environment
exam: Reduced social engagement that is not accompanied by restricted interests or repetitive behaviors

differential.name: Selective mutism
differential.why_considered: A child who does not speak in some settings may be thought to have a communication disorder.

history: Speaks normally in at least one setting, usually at home
Consistent failure to speak in specific social situations where speaking is expected
No restricted interests or repetitive behaviors
exam: Normal social communication and joint attention when comfortable

differential.name: Landau-Kleffner syndrome
differential.why_considered: Loss of language skills in a previously normally developing child can be mistaken for autistic regression.
differential.trigger: Loss of previously acquired language in a child with seizures or abnormal EEG

history: Loss of language after a period of normal development
Seizures or episodic behavioral changes
Language regression rather than gradual social-communication differences
exam: Social interest often preserved early in the course
labs: EEG showing epileptiform activity, especially during sleep

differential.name: Rett syndrome
differential.why_considered: A genetic disorder with developmental regression, loss of hand skills and social withdrawal that can resemble autism.
differential.trigger: A girl with regression, loss of purposeful hand use and stereotyped hand movements

history: Normal development for the first 6–18 months followed by regression
Loss of purposeful hand skills and spoken language
Deceleration of head growth
exam: Gait abnormalities or loss of ambulation

severity.mild: Requires support: social-communication difficulties are noticeable but the person can speak in full sentences, has some friendships and can manage most daily activities with support; restricted interests and repetitive behaviors are present but not disabling.
severity.moderate: Requires substantial support: marked deficits in verbal and nonverbal social communication, obvious distress with change, restricted or repetitive behaviors that interfere with functioning in several settings, and need for support with daily activities.
severity.severe: Requires very substantial support: minimal or no spoken language, severe deficits in social communication, extreme inflexibility and distress with change, and repetitive behaviors that markedly interfere with functioning; often accompanied by intellectual disability and need for help with most daily activities.
severity.critical: Not applicable; autism spectrum disorder itself is not a life-threatening condition, though a person may present acutely with injury, seizure, severe agitation or self-injury.

red_flags.finding: Loss of previously acquired language or social skills
red_flags.meaning: Regression should prompt evaluation for a neurodegenerative, metabolic or epileptic cause such as Landau-Kleffner syndrome or Rett syndrome

red_flags.finding: No response to name or no social smiling by 12 months
red_flags.meaning: Early social-communication red flag that warrants developmental screening and evaluation

red_flags.finding: No pointing or joint attention by 18 months
red_flags.meaning: Early red flag for autism spectrum disorder; needs comprehensive evaluation
Language delay that requires hearing testing and developmental evaluation

red_flags.finding: New focal neurologic deficit, macrocephaly or seizures
red_flags.meaning: Suggests a structural, genetic or metabolic cause and warrants brain imaging and further workup
Risk of injury; needs urgent behavioral and safety assessment

complications.name: Intellectual disability
clues: Global developmental delays beyond social communication

complications.name: Anxiety disorders
clues: Distress with change or social demands

complications.name: Social isolation and difficulty maintaining employment
clues: Difficulties with social demands at school or work

special_populations.differences: Symptoms are usually recognized in the second year of life; younger children may present only with delayed language, lack of pointing or joint attention, and repetitive play. Early diagnosis and intervention improve outcomes.
May show reduced babbling, poor eye contact, lack of social smiling and not turning to name by 9–12 months; diagnosis is usually not made before 18–24 months.
Adults may have learned to mask social difficulties and present with anxiety, depression or social exhaustion rather than obvious autistic behaviors; diagnosis may be made late in life.

key_questions.question: When did you first notice that something was different about your child's development?
key_questions.looking_for: Concerns noticed in the first two years of life; gradual onset rather than a sudden change

key_questions.question: Does your child respond when you call their name?
key_questions.looking_for: Not turning or orienting to name, especially by 12 months

key_questions.question: Does your child point at things or follow where you point to share interest?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent pointing or joint attention by 18 months

key_questions.question: How does your child communicate needs — words, gestures, pulling your hand, or leading you to things?
key_questions.looking_for: Fewer words than expected for age, absent phrase speech, echolalia, or unusual use of another person's hand as a tool

key_questions.question: Does your child make eye contact with you or with other people?
key_questions.looking_for: Reduced or absent eye contact and limited shared attention

key_questions.question: Does your child have routines or rituals, and how do they react when those change?
key_questions.looking_for: Insistence on sameness and marked distress with small changes

key_questions.question: Does your child have any repetitive movements, like hand flapping, rocking or spinning?
key_questions.looking_for: Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements

key_questions.question: What does your child like to play with, and do they have very intense or narrow interests?
key_questions.looking_for: Restricted, fixated interests or play limited to parts of objects

key_questions.question: How does your child react to loud noises, bright lights, certain textures or smells?
key_questions.looking_for: Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input

key_questions.question: Has your child ever lost skills they previously had, such as words or social skills?
key_questions.looking_for: Regression, which should prompt evaluation for a neurodegenerative, metabolic or epileptic cause

key_questions.question: How does your child do with other children — do they make and keep friends?
key_questions.looking_for: Difficulty developing, maintaining and understanding relationships

key_questions.question: How is your child's sleep? Any trouble falling asleep or waking at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Sleep problems, which are common and treatable

key_questions.question: How is your child's eating? Any constipation or stomach complaints?
key_questions.looking_for: Feeding selectivity, constipation or other gastrointestinal symptoms

key_questions.question: Has your child had any seizures or staring spells?
key_questions.looking_for: Seizures, which occur in a minority and warrant EEG

key_questions.question: Did your child pass their newborn hearing screen, and have they had a hearing test since?
key_questions.looking_for: Hearing loss as a treatable cause of language and social delay

key_questions.question: Were there any complications around birth — preterm delivery, very low birth weight or time in the NICU?
key_questions.looking_for: Preterm birth or very low birth weight as a risk factor

key_questions.question: Did you take any medications during pregnancy, especially valproate or thalidomide?
key_questions.looking_for: In utero exposure to valproate or thalidomide

key_questions.question: Does anyone in the family have autism, a learning disability, language delay or intellectual disability?
key_questions.looking_for: A sibling or first-degree relative with autism spectrum disorder or related conditions

key_questions.question: Who first raised concerns about your child's development — you, a teacher or a childcare provider?
key_questions.looking_for: Concerns noticed by parents or early childhood educators when milestones are not met

key_questions.question: Are the difficulties present in more than one setting, like home and school?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms across settings rather than limited to one environment

accepted_names: Pervasive developmental disorder not otherwise specified
reasoning_points: Persistent deficits in social communication and social interaction across multiple settings
Deficits in social-emotional reciprocity, such as not responding to name or not sharing interests
Deficits in nonverbal communication used for social interaction, such as reduced eye contact and absent pointing or joint attention
Deficits in developing, maintaining and understanding relationships, such as difficulty making friends
Restricted, repetitive patterns of behavior, interests or activities
Stereotyped or repetitive motor movements, use of objects or speech
Insistence on sameness, inflexible adherence to routines or ritualized patterns
Highly restricted, fixated interests that are abnormal in intensity or focus
Hyper- or hyporeactivity to sensory input or unusual interest in sensory aspects of the environment
Symptoms present in early development and causing significant impairment in functioning
Symptoms not better explained by intellectual disability or global developmental delay
Hearing loss excluded with audiologic testing before attributing language delay to autism spectrum disorder
Diagnosis made from developmental history and behavior, since there is no confirmatory blood test
Standardized tools such as the M-CHAT-R/F screen and ADOS-2 or ADI-R support the diagnosis
Genetic testing such as chromosomal microarray and fragile X testing offered after diagnosis

easy: Toddler with no words, no response to name and no pointing
Parent describes hand flapping, lining up toys and distress when routines change
Reduced eye contact and no joint attention on exam
Normal hearing screen and normal neurologic exam
Clear early developmental concerns documented at well-child visits
medium: School-age child with fluent speech but difficulty with back-and-forth conversation and friendships
Intense narrow interests and insistence on sameness without obvious language delay
Symptoms noticed mainly when social demands increase at preschool or school
Co-occurring ADHD or anxiety that partly masks the social-communication deficits
Girl who masks social difficulties and presents with anxiety or social exhaustion
hard: Toddler presenting only with delayed language and repetitive play, without a clear description of social difficulty
Child with intellectual disability where delays are global and it is unclear whether autism is also present
Adolescent or adult diagnosed late after years of masking, presenting with depression or social exhaustion
Child with regression, seizures or focal findings raising concern for Rett syndrome or Landau-Kleffner syndrome
Child with a history of severe neglect or institutional care raising reactive attachment disorder
Child who does not speak in some settings, raising selective mutism
